title: THE PROPHET WHO EXPOSED ADULTERY IN THE PULPIT—AND THE LIES THAT MADE GOD’S PEOPLE FEEL SAFE WHILE THEY WERE DYING SPIRITUALLY
paragraphs: THE PROPHET WHO EXPOSED ADULTERY IN THE PULPIT—AND THE LIES THAT MADE GOD’S PEOPLE FEEL SAFE WHILE THEY WERE DYING SPIRITUALLY

Jeremiah 23:10–14 | When the voices claiming to speak for God were leading people away from Him, one grieving prophet dared to expose what everyone else was afraid to confront. But the most terrifying part of this story is not what happened thousands of years ago. It is how easily the same deception can happen today.
What if the person telling you that everything is fine with your soul is the very person helping you drift away from God?
What if the message that makes you feel most comfortable is the message you most desperately need to question?

And what if the greatest danger to your faith is not someone openly telling you to abandon Jesus, but someone repeatedly assuring you that you can follow Him without ever surrendering the sin that is destroying you?
There was a time in Israel's history when people still spoke about God.
Religious leaders still occupied positions of influence. Prophets still delivered messages. Sacred language still filled the mouths of those who claimed spiritual authority.
But something was terribly wrong.

Behind the appearance of religion, hearts were wandering. Truth was being compromised. Sin was being normalized. And people entrusted with speaking God's Word were becoming part of the very corruption they should have confronted.
Then God raised up a man named Jeremiah.
He was not sent to entertain the crowd.
He was not sent to protect the reputation of corrupt leaders.
He was not sent to make rebellion sound respectable.
He was sent to speak the truth, even when that truth would break his own heart.
And what God revealed through him should make every preacher, every ministry leader, and every person who calls themselves a Christian examine their soul.
Because Jeremiah did not merely expose adultery.
He exposed what happens when people use the name of God while refusing to submit to the Word of God.
And before this story is finished, we must face an uncomfortable question.
Are we following the living God—or merely following the voices that tell us what we want to hear?
Jeremiah 23:10 begins with a devastating declaration.
“For the land is full of adulterers; for because of swearing the land mourneth; the pleasant places of the wilderness are dried up, and their course is evil, and their force is not right.” (KJV)
Read those words slowly.
The land was full of adulterers.
The land was mourning.
Evil had become a way of life.
And the strength people possessed was being directed toward what was wrong.
This was not simply Jeremiah expressing personal disappointment with society. He was delivering God's indictment against a people whose covenant unfaithfulness had spread through the land.
The Hebrew text begins with the words:
כִּי מְנָאֲפִים מָלְאָה הָאָרֶץ
Ki mena'afim male'ah ha'aretz.
“For the land is full of adulterers.”
The word mena'afim comes from the Hebrew verb נָאַף (na'aph), meaning to commit adultery.
That matters.
Because we must not soften the accusation until it loses its force.
The passage is not merely saying that the people had developed unhealthy spiritual habits. Adultery was a serious violation of God's covenant commands, and Jeremiah deliberately uses that language.
Throughout the prophetic writings, marital unfaithfulness also becomes a powerful picture of covenant betrayal against the Lord.
God's people had been called to belong to Him.
Yet their hearts had pursued what He had forbidden.
The language confronts both the moral corruption present among the people and the wider tragedy of their unfaithfulness to God.
But there is an important detail we must not overlook.
Jeremiah 23:10 speaks about the condition of the land. The following verses narrow the accusation to prophets and priests, and verse 14 explicitly identifies adultery among Jerusalem's prophets.
We should not claim that every priest or prophet was personally guilty of sexual adultery. The passage condemns pervasive wickedness and specifically exposes corrupt spiritual leaders.
That distinction matters because biblical truth does not need exaggeration to become powerful.
It is already powerful.
And here is what makes this passage so frightening.
The people who should have been helping others recognize sin were themselves participating in corruption.
Imagine the heartbreak.
Someone comes looking for spiritual direction.
They are struggling.
Their marriage is collapsing. Their conscience is troubled. Their secret habits are consuming them. Their heart knows something is wrong.
They need truth.
They need repentance.
They need someone who loves them enough to point them back to God.
But instead, they encounter voices that make disobedience sound harmless.
Voices that offer reassurance without repentance.
Voices that protect the appearance of religion while leaving the soul in danger.
That is not spiritual care.
That is betrayal.
And Jeremiah's next words reveal just how deep the corruption had become.
“For both prophet and priest are profane; yea, in my house have I found their wickedness, saith the LORD.” (Jeremiah 23:11, KJV)
“In my house.”
Those three words should make us tremble.
God was not merely confronting wickedness in distant places.
He was exposing wickedness connected with His own house.
The Hebrew word translated “profane” is חָנֵף (chaneph), which carries the sense of being godless, impious, or morally corrupt.
These were people associated with sacred responsibilities, yet their conduct contradicted the holiness of the God they claimed to serve.
Their religious position did not make their wickedness acceptable.
Their spiritual vocabulary did not make their hearts faithful.
Their public influence did not place them beyond divine accountability.
And that truth has not expired.
A microphone does not make someone holy.
A religious title does not make someone trustworthy.
A large following does not prove that God approves of a message.
A beautiful worship service cannot make deliberate disobedience righteous.
And the ability to quote Scripture does not guarantee that a person is submitting to Scripture.
Jesus Himself warned that some would call Him “Lord, Lord” while failing to do the will of His Father (Matthew 7:21–23).
That should humble every one of us.
Because it is possible to become familiar with the language of faith while resisting the Lord to whom that language points.
It is possible to know when to say “Amen” while refusing to obey the truth being affirmed.
It is possible to look spiritually alive before people while carrying a heart that has grown cold toward God.
And perhaps that is why this passage hurts.
Because it does not allow us to examine religious leaders without examining ourselves.
We can recognize hypocrisy in someone else and still excuse it in our own lives.
We can condemn public scandals while quietly negotiating with private sin.
We can demand integrity from the pulpit while refusing honesty in our homes.
But God sees beyond appearances.
He sees what is hidden.
And His knowledge is not limited by the reputation we have carefully built.
Then comes the warning in Jeremiah 23:12.

“Wherefore their way shall be unto them as slippery ways in the darkness: they shall be driven on, and fall therein: for I will bring evil upon them, even the year of their visitation, saith the LORD.” (KJV)
Picture someone walking along a narrow, slippery path in complete darkness.
There is no stable footing.
No clear direction.
Every step carries danger.
And the person keeps moving as though nothing is wrong.
That is the picture God gives of the judgment awaiting these corrupt leaders.
Their way would become slippery.
Their darkness would not protect them.
Their position would not rescue them.
God's appointed time of reckoning would come.
There is a terrifying difference between being temporarily successful and being spiritually safe.
Sometimes people mistake the absence of immediate consequences for the approval of God.
The ministry is still growing.
The money is still coming.
The applause has not stopped.
The audience still believes.
So they assume everything must be fine.
But Scripture never teaches that outward success is proof of inward faithfulness.
And delayed judgment is not divine permission.
The apostle Paul later warned:
“Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.” (Galatians 6:7, KJV)
Yet even here, we must understand the heart of biblical warning.
God does not expose sin merely to satisfy our curiosity about someone else's downfall.
His warnings also summon hearers to repentance.
The proper response to Jeremiah 23 is not to become addicted to scandal.
It is to become serious about holiness.
Because a person can spend years exposing the sins of others while never surrendering their own.
And that is another kind of spiritual blindness.
Then Jeremiah makes a comparison that would have shaken his original audience.
In verse 13, God speaks about the prophets of Samaria.
He says they prophesied by Baal and caused His people Israel to err.
Baal was a false deity worshiped in the ancient Near East, and the reference recalls the idolatry that corrupted the northern kingdom.
The prophets of Samaria had led people astray through false worship.
But then comes verse 14.
And the accusation becomes even more disturbing.

“I have seen also in the prophets of Jerusalem an horrible thing: they commit adultery, and walk in lies: they strengthen also the hands of evildoers, that none doth return from his wickedness...” (Jeremiah 23:14, KJV)
Stop there.
“They strengthen also the hands of evildoers.”
That may be one of the most heartbreaking accusations in the entire passage.
The prophets were not merely failing to confront wickedness.
They were strengthening those who practiced it.
The Hebrew phrase is:
וְחִזְּקוּ יְדֵי מְרֵעִים
Vechizzequ yedei mere'im.
“They strengthened the hands of evildoers.”
The verb comes from חָזַק (chazaq), meaning to be strong or to strengthen.
In this context, the leaders were reinforcing people in their wrongdoing instead of calling them away from it.
And the consequence is stated plainly.
“That none doth return from his wickedness.”
The Hebrew verb behind “return” is שׁוּב (shuv), one of the great words of the Old Testament.
It means to turn back or return.
In prophetic calls to repentance, it describes turning away from wickedness and returning to the Lord.
This is what makes the accusation so serious.
The false prophets were doing the opposite of what faithful spiritual leadership should do.
Instead of helping people turn back, they were helping people remain where they were.
Instead of confronting rebellion, they were reinforcing it.
Instead of speaking words that could awaken a hardened conscience, they were encouraging people to continue in darkness.
And that brings us to a question every generation must face.
What happens when spiritual encouragement becomes permission to remain unchanged?
Encouragement is good.
Comfort is necessary.
Grace is glorious.
But biblical encouragement never requires us to pretend that sin is harmless.
And biblical grace never teaches that we should make peace with the very things Christ died to save us from.
Romans 6:1–2 confronts the idea that grace gives believers permission to continue in sin.
Paul asks whether we should continue in sin so grace may abound.
His answer is unmistakable.
“God forbid.”
Grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace brings us to the Savior who forgives, cleanses, and transforms.
There is a difference between comforting someone who is fighting sin and reassuring someone that they never need to fight it.
There is a difference between patiently walking beside a struggling believer and telling that believer that obedience no longer matters.
There is a difference between proclaiming God's mercy and using God's mercy as an excuse to silence His commands.
One leads people toward Christ.
The other can leave them comfortable in bondage.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly what that bondage feels like.
You still believe in God.
You still pray sometimes.
You still listen to worship music.
You still share Bible verses.
But there is something in your life you have been hiding.
Something you keep promising to surrender.
Something that has quietly gained power over your decisions.
Maybe it is an adulterous relationship.
Maybe it is pornography.
Maybe it is dishonesty.
Maybe it is bitterness you have been feeding for years.
Maybe it is greed, manipulation, pride, or a secret life that contradicts the person everyone thinks you are.
You have learned how to function while carrying it.
You have learned how to smile while concealing it.
You have learned how to look spiritually healthy while feeling increasingly distant from God.
And the most dangerous thing someone could tell you right now is that you never need to confront it.
Because the sin you refuse to bring into the light will not become harmless simply because you have learned to live around it.
But listen carefully.
Being convicted by God's Word does not mean you are beyond His mercy.
The purpose of this message is not to convince you that you are too filthy to approach Jesus.
It is to remind you that you do not have to keep running from the only Savior who can cleanse you.
And that is where this ancient prophetic warning begins to lead us toward the hope of the Gospel.
Jeremiah 23 does not end with the exposure of corrupt prophets.
The chapter eventually turns toward an extraordinary promise.
God speaks of raising up a righteous Branch from David's line.
“Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth.” (Jeremiah 23:5, KJV)
Do you see the contrast?
Corrupt leaders had failed.
False prophets had misled.
Those entrusted with spiritual responsibility had betrayed their calling.
But God promised a righteous King.
A King who would not walk in lies.
A King who would not strengthen wickedness.
A King who would rule with justice and righteousness.
Christians understand this promised Davidic King to find His fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
And suddenly the story becomes much greater than an ancient scandal.
Because the answer to corrupt spiritual leadership is not merely finding a more impressive religious personality.
The ultimate answer is Jesus.
The righteous King.
The faithful Shepherd.
The One who speaks truth without deception and extends mercy without compromising holiness.
Jesus did not come to flatter sinners into spiritual complacency.
He came to save sinners.
And salvation is more beautiful than being told that our rebellion does not matter.
Think about the woman caught in adultery in John 8.

The account, traditionally included in John 7:53–8:11, has a well-known textual history: it is absent from the earliest surviving manuscripts of John's Gospel and appears in different locations in some later witnesses. That should be acknowledged rather than concealed.
In the traditional account, Jesus refuses to join a merciless crowd in condemning the woman.
But He also does not celebrate her sin.
He says:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” (John 8:11, KJV)
Mercy.
And a call to leave sin.
Compassion.
And truth.
Jesus does not treat human beings as disposable because they have fallen.
Neither does He pretend that the things destroying them are good.
This union of grace and truth is central to His character.
John 1:14 describes Him as full of grace and truth.
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Both.
Perfectly.
And this is where we must be especially careful not to misunderstand Jeremiah's warning.
The passage does not give religious leaders permission to humiliate people, invent accusations, or control others through fear.
It does not justify treating every struggling Christian as a hypocrite.
It does not make spiritual abuse acceptable.
A faithful shepherd must speak truth, but must also care for the wounded.
Galatians 6:1 calls spiritually mature believers to restore someone caught in sin with gentleness, while watching themselves.
That is the difference between biblical correction and religious cruelty.
One seeks restoration.
The other seeks domination.
One points to Christ.
The other makes the accuser the center of attention.
And we must never confuse the two.
Because Jesus did not die to create a community where sinners are terrified to confess their struggles.
He died to redeem a people who walk in the light of His grace and truth.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Read that again.
To forgive us.
And to cleanse us.
Not merely to help us manage our public image.
Not merely to make us feel temporarily better.
But to forgive and cleanse.
That is the hope false prophets cannot provide.
A comforting lie can temporarily quiet your conscience.
But only Jesus can reconcile you to God.
A religious performance can impress other people.
But only Jesus can make you righteous before the Father through faith in Him.
A spiritual leader can offer advice.
But only Jesus is the Savior.
And when He saves, He does not leave us to fight sin in our own strength.
He gives His people the Holy Spirit, who works in them to produce genuine transformation.
This is why the Gospel is not simply the announcement that God overlooks everything.
It is the announcement that Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
The sin that deserves judgment was not treated as insignificant.
It was so serious that the Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
And the love of God was so great that He did.
Now consider the cross.
The innocent One was condemned.
The righteous One suffered.
The sinless One bore the sins of others.
Jesus did not walk in lies.
He is the truth.
He did not commit adultery.
He remained faithful.
He did not strengthen people in wickedness.
He called sinners to repentance and offered them forgiveness.
He did not exploit the weak.
He laid down His life for His sheep.
And when He rose from the dead, He proved that sin and death would not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
That is why our message is not simply about scandal.
It is about grace.
Not cheap grace that excuses everything.
But costly grace purchased through the blood of Jesus Christ.
Grace that receives the repentant.
Grace that restores the broken.
Grace that teaches us to deny ungodliness, as Titus 2:11–12 declares.
Grace that makes a new life possible.
But notice what that means.
Jesus does not rewrite the truth to accommodate our sin.
He transforms sinners through the truth of His Gospel.
He does not call darkness light.
He brings people out of darkness.
He does not promise that repentance will erase every earthly consequence.
He promises forgiveness and new life to those who come to Him in faith.
And sometimes that new life begins with a confession you have been avoiding.
A conversation you have been postponing.
A relationship you need to end.
A lie you need to correct.
A wrong you need to make right.
A secret you need to bring into the light.
Maybe you need to stop defending the person who has been misleading you spiritually.
Maybe you need to stop treating every correction as an attack.
Maybe you need to open your Bible again and ask whether the messages you have been believing actually agree with what God has spoken.
And maybe you need to admit something you have not dared to say aloud.
You are tired.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of the divided life.
Tired of asking God for peace while refusing to surrender what is stealing it.
If that is you, please hear this.
You do not have to clean yourself up before coming to Christ.
Come to Him honestly.
Confess what is true.
Turn away from what is wrong.
Trust the Savior who died and rose again.
Seek help from trustworthy, mature believers who will walk with you in truth and gentleness.
And remember that the road of Christian growth is not always a straight line of uninterrupted victories.
Real believers can struggle.
Real believers can stumble.
But the answer is not to surrender to the darkness.
It is to keep returning to Christ.
The same Lord who calls you to holiness is the Lord who supplies grace for the journey.
And if you are a pastor, preacher, teacher, ministry leader, or someone with spiritual influence, Jeremiah 23 carries an especially solemn responsibility.
People are not yours to manipulate.
Their consciences are not yours to control.
Their generosity is not yours to exploit.
Their trust is not yours to betray.
You are accountable for what you teach.
You are accountable for how you treat those entrusted to your care.
You must not use the promise of blessing to disguise greed.
You must not use the language of grace to protect unrepentant wickedness.
And you must never make loyalty to your ministry a substitute for loyalty to Jesus Christ.
The people of God need shepherds who love the truth more than applause.
Who would rather lose popularity than distort Scripture.
Who understand that wounded people need compassion, and wandering people need faithful correction.
Who remember that the church belongs to Christ.
Not to a personality.
Not to a platform.
Not to a brand.
To Christ.
And for those who have been hurt by corrupt spiritual leadership, this matters too.
The failure of someone who claimed to represent God is not proof that Jesus has failed you.
The betrayal may have been real.
The damage may have been deep.
The grief may still be difficult to explain.
You may have trusted someone who used Scripture to protect their own wrongdoing.
You may have been told to remain silent when you should have been protected.
You may have watched people defend a reputation while ignoring those who were wounded.
God does not require you to call evil good.
And forgiveness does not mean abandoning wisdom, accountability, justice, or appropriate boundaries.
Jeremiah 23 itself reminds us that God sees the wickedness of corrupt leaders.
He is not indifferent.
He is not deceived by religious appearances.
And His righteousness is not compromised by the failures of those who misuse His name.
So do not confuse the counterfeit with the Savior.
Do not let the betrayal of a human shepherd convince you that the Good Shepherd cannot be trusted.
Jesus said in John 10:11:
“I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.” (KJV)
False shepherds may use the sheep to protect themselves.
Jesus gave Himself for His sheep.
That difference changes everything.
And now, after walking through Jeremiah's warning, there is one question that remains.
Not whether we can identify the failures of religious leaders in the past.
Not whether we can name every false teacher on the internet.
Not whether we can win an argument about someone else's theology.
But whether we ourselves are willing to be corrected by the Word of God.
When Scripture exposes something in your life, do you surrender it—or search for a voice that will excuse it?
That question reaches beyond the pulpit.
It reaches into our bedrooms.
Our marriages.
Our finances.
Our private messages.
Our browsing histories.
Our motives.
Our hidden compromises.
Our treatment of the people who cannot offer us anything in return.
It reaches into the places where we are most tempted to say, “God understands,” when what we really mean is, “I do not want to change.”
Yes, God understands.
He understands our weakness.
He understands our wounds.
He understands the battles no one else sees.
But He also understands the destruction sin brings.
And because He loves us, He does not invite us to remain enslaved to it.
The call of Jesus is not an invitation to pretend.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
Maybe this is the moment you stop running.
Maybe this is the moment you stop blaming everyone else.
Maybe this is the moment you finally say, “Lord, I have been wrong. I need Your mercy. Teach me to walk in Your truth.”
There is no shame in admitting that you need a Savior.
The tragedy is not that you have discovered your need.
The tragedy would be refusing the One who came to meet it.
Not as a performance.
Not because public confession earns forgiveness.
He does not.
But because sometimes a simple, honest response becomes the beginning of a meaningful conversation with brothers and sisters who are also learning to walk in the light.
Your story may remind someone else that repentance is possible and that God's mercy is real.
There is also someone in your life who may need this message.
Perhaps a friend who has become discouraged by religious hypocrisy.
A family member who has been confusing religious activity with a relationship with Jesus.
A believer who is struggling to distinguish biblical grace from permission to continue in sin.
Or someone who has walked away from church because they were wounded by people who claimed to speak for God.
Because faith should not be built on emotional moments alone.
It needs roots.
It needs Scripture.
It needs prayer.
It needs a community where truth is spoken in love.
And that is also why the Gospel Warrior mission matters to us.
We want to keep creating Scripture-centered articles, biblical teaching, devotional reflections, and discipleship resources that help people grow deeper in their understanding of Jesus Christ.
Those free resources are part of our desire to make biblical learning and spiritual nourishment accessible.
But creating, maintaining, and expanding this work also requires real resources.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful, not extracted through guilt or pressure.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
And that is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not because financial support proves that you love Jesus more than someone who cannot afford it.
And certainly not because the Gospel is for sale.
The Gospel is God's gift of grace, received through faith in Jesus Christ.
These products are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
But they can serve as useful resources, meaningful gifts, and reminders of the truths we are learning together.
Your prayers matter.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
Your commitment to living out the Gospel matters.
And no amount of money can replace obedience, integrity, love, or faithfulness to Jesus.
We do not want to build a community that merely applauds powerful messages.
We want to encourage a community that opens the Bible after reading them.
A community that examines every teaching by Scripture.
A community that refuses to defend spiritual deception simply because the person speaking is popular.
A community that has room for broken people, but does not celebrate what is breaking them.
A community where repentance is not treated as humiliation, but as a gracious return to the Lord.
And above all, a community that remembers that Jesus Christ is the center of everything.
Jeremiah stood before a generation surrounded by religious language and spiritual corruption.
He exposed adultery.
He confronted lies.
He warned those who strengthened evildoers.
And through that same chapter, God announced the coming of a righteous King.
That is the beautiful contrast we must never forget.
Human leaders can fail.
Religious institutions can become corrupted.
Public reputations can collapse.
But Jesus Christ remains righteous.
His truth does not change when a preacher falls.
His mercy does not disappear when a believer stumbles.
His Gospel does not lose its power when someone misrepresents it.
And His invitation still stands.
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Him.
Walk in the light.
Because the greatest miracle is not that a sinner learns how to look religious.
It is that a sinner, forgiven by grace, begins to become a new creation in Christ.
So before you leave this article, consider one final question.
If Jesus exposed the truth about your heart today, would you ask Him to hide it from everyone—or would you ask Him to heal what He revealed?
You do not have to answer that publicly.
But answer it honestly before God.
And remember this:
The lie that keeps you comfortable in darkness can never love you the way the Savior who calls you into the light already does.
